To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of complications from circumcision is high in Africa, that circumcision would be a very costly HIV prevention method, that circumcision would reduce the HIV risk of men who are already HIV positive, and that circumcision would not reduce the risk of HIV transmission to women by circumcised men. (author's)

1) the cost of circumcision is much greater than the cost of condoms; 2) circumcision is much less effective than condoms at preventing HIV transmission; 3) the cost effectiveness of circumcision is much lower than the cost effectiveness of condoms; and 4) circumcision is a very poor substitute for condoms, and should not be used as a substitute. A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
circumcision is not a magic bullet.
the costs of circumcision are high, and that the cost effectiveness of circumcision is low.
circumcision is an effective intervention to reduce the incidence of HIV in Africa.
The main takeaway from our work is that
circumcision is not the magic bullet that many people thought it was, says study coauthor David Wilson, an epidemiologist at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine.
circumcision is an important part of the HIV prevention tool kit but it is not the most cost effective way to prevent HIV in Africa.
circumcision is not a silver bullet.
